Inversion Demo

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: No one wins here: the picture shows what each coloured circle turns into inside the big circle.
How to play: Drag O or A to change the big circle, drag a coloured circle or its two dots to change that circle, and press "Add circle" or "Remove last circle". You can also press Tab and use the arrow keys on any dot.
Look for the math

The big circle is the "mirror". Its centre is O and A sits on its rim. Every other circle has its own photograph in this mirror, drawn dashed. Drag a circle and its photograph moves in a way that seems strange at first, but nothing about it is random.

Each point hops along a line through O

In inversion in a circle of radius R, a point X and its image X′ lie on the same ray from O with OX × OX′ = R². Near points go far and far points come near; O itself has no image. The logic test checked this product and the distance rule P′Q′ = R² PQ / (OP × OQ) on 500 pairs of points.

A circle becomes a circle — or a line

Write d for the distance from O to a circle's centre and r for that circle's radius. Its image is a circle with centre on the same ray, scaled by k = R² / (d² − r²), and radius |k| r. When the circle goes through O, d² = r² and the formula breaks down: the image is a straight line. Both claims on the page were checked on hundreds of circles, including sample points that must land on the image. The old applet switches to the line drawing a little early, whenever |d² − r²| ≤ 100 in its 600 by 450 drawing; that is a drawing tolerance, kept here so the picture matches the applet.

Circles at right angles do not change

A circle whose tangents meet the big circle at right angles satisfies d² = R² + r². Then k = 1, so its image is exactly itself. The page calls these circles invariant, and the logic test confirmed it for 400 such circles. Because angles keep their size, inversion is a conformal map: invert twice and you are back where you started.

What changed from the old page

The original page is "Inversion Tool". A 2006 capture shows the Java applet named InversionDemo embedded there; today the same cut-the-knot page runs a GeoGebra remake with the same wording. This port follows the Java code: the same starting points, the same random circle sizes and colours, and the same image formula. The colours and drag limits were adjusted for dark mode and for fingers on a phone; the mathematics was not.

Press Add circle twice, then drag a coloured circle until its centre passes through O: watch its dashed image straighten into a line. Drag it back and the line curls up into a circle again.
